content.what_text: A percentage is a mathematical concept that represents a fraction of 100. The word itself comes from the Latin phrase 'per centum', meaning 'by the hundred'. Percentages are one of the most fundamental concepts used in everyday mathematics, finance, science, and data analysis. They provide a universal way to express proportions, making it easy to compare values of different scales on a common basis.

content.section1_text: Percentage calculations are essential in countless real-world scenarios. Whether you're calculating a tip at a restaurant, figuring out how much you'll save during a sale, determining your exam score, or analyzing business growth metrics, percentages are everywhere. Our calculator handles three main types of percentage calculations: finding a percentage of a number (e.g., What is 25% of 200?), calculating percentage change between two values (e.g., The price went from $50 to $65, what's the increase?), and determining what percentage one number is of another (e.g., 15 is what percent of 75?).
content.section2_text: The basic percentage formula is straightforward: Percentage = (Part / Whole) × 100. For example, if you scored 45 out of 60 on a test, your percentage score would be (45 / 60) × 100 = 75%. For percentage change, the formula is: Percentage Change = ((New Value - Old Value) / Old Value) × 100. A positive result indicates an increase, while a negative result indicates a decrease. Understanding these formulas helps you verify calculations and apply percentage concepts in new situations.
content.section3_title: Common Uses of Percentages in Daily Life

section3_items.title: Shopping & Discounts
section3_items.text: Retailers use percentages to advertise discounts. A 30% off sale on a $120 item means you save $36 and pay $84. Understanding percentage discounts helps you make smarter purchasing decisions and compare deals across different stores.

section3_items.title: Finance & Banking
section3_items.text: Interest rates on savings accounts, loans, and credit cards are all expressed as percentages. A 5% annual interest rate on a $10,000 savings account means you earn $500 per year. Compound interest builds on this concept, making percentages crucial for financial planning.

section3_items.title: Grades & Academics
section3_items.text: Academic performance is typically measured in percentages. Understanding how to calculate your percentage score helps you track your progress, set academic goals, and determine what scores you need on future assignments to achieve your target grade.

section3_items.title: Health & Nutrition
section3_items.text: Daily value percentages on food labels tell you how much of a recommended daily nutrient intake a serving provides. A food item with 20% daily value of calcium means one serving provides one-fifth of your recommended daily calcium intake.

section3_items.title: Business & Economics
section3_items.text: Businesses use percentages to measure growth rates, profit margins, market share, employee performance, and customer satisfaction. Year-over-year revenue growth of 15% indicates healthy business expansion.

section3_items.title: Statistics & Data Analysis
section3_items.text: Percentages are fundamental in statistical analysis for expressing probabilities, confidence intervals, error margins, and survey results. They make complex data accessible and comparable to a wide audience.

content.section4_title: Tips for Quick Mental Percentage Calculations
section4_items: To find 10% of any number, simply move the decimal point one place to the left (10% of 250 = 25)
To find 5%, calculate 10% first and then divide by 2 (5% of 250 = 12.5)
To find 25%, divide the number by 4 (25% of 200 = 50)
To find 1%, move the decimal point two places to the left (1% of 350 = 3.5)
To find 33%, divide the number by 3 (33% of 90 = 30)
Combine these tricks for complex percentages: 15% = 10% + 5% (15% of 200 = 20 + 10 = 30)

examples.label: Sales Tax
examples.desc: Calculating 8.5% sales tax on a $150 purchase: $150 × 0.085 = $12.75. Total cost = $162.75.

examples.label: Restaurant Tip
examples.desc: A 15% tip on an $80 dinner: $80 × 0.15 = $12.00. For quick mental math, find 10% ($8) and add half of that ($4).

examples.label: Discount Shopping
examples.desc: 25% off a $200 item: $200 × 0.25 = $50 savings. You pay $150 instead of $200.

examples.label: Salary Increase
examples.desc: A 7% raise on a $50,000 salary: $50,000 × 0.07 = $3,500. New salary = $53,500 per year.

faqs.q: How do I calculate percentage increase?
faqs.a: Use the formula: ((New Value - Old Value) / Old Value) × 100. For example, if a stock price goes from $40 to $52, the increase is ((52-40)/40) × 100 = 30%.

faqs.q: What is the difference between percentage and percentile?
faqs.a: A percentage represents a part of a whole out of 100, while a percentile indicates the value below which a given percentage of observations fall. For example, scoring in the 90th percentile means you scored better than 90% of test-takers.

faqs.q: Can a percentage be more than 100%?
faqs.a: Yes! A percentage over 100% indicates a value greater than the reference whole. For example, if your investment doubles from $1,000 to $2,000, that's a 100% increase. If it goes to $3,000, that's a 200% increase.

faqs.q: How do I convert a fraction to a percentage?
faqs.a: Divide the numerator by the denominator and multiply by 100. For example, 3/8 = 0.375 × 100 = 37.5%.
